| ABSTRACT: Using a small open economy overlapping generations model, this paper examines how AI can drive economic divergence across and within Asian economies. While AI adoption may promise sizable productivity gains, it could create temporary but potentially longlasting divergence across countries. Structurally-prepared advanced economies tend to adopt AI earlier and see immediate growth gains while emerging markets and developing economies (EMDEs) face delayed adoption and initial growth headwinds from rising costs of capital. Structural reforms that boost productivity and strengthen human capital not only accelerate adoption in EMDEs but also amplify the growth gains. Within countries, AI adoption could widen inequality along multiple dimensions: across skill groups, as high-skilled workers benefit disproportionately from complementarity with the more capital-intensive technology, and across generation, as the shift of national income toward capital favors asset-rich older households relative to younger workers who rely primarily on labor income. Redistributive policies can help mitigate these distributional pressures, though they entail equity efficiency trade-offs that vary with country-specific fiscal and demographic conditions. | |

1 Introduction

Asia’s remarkable economic success over the past few decades now faces fundamental 
challenges. The region’s potential growth is projected to decline over the medium term as 
demographic dividends disappear and productivity growth stagnates (Che et al., 2025; 
IMF, 2024). Working-age populations across Northeast Asia are projected to shrink by 
over 200 million by 2050 (United Nations, 2024), while global trade tensions and reshoring 
pressures threaten the export-led strategies that transformed the region into the world’s 
manufacturing hub. 
Artificial Intelligence (AI) holds the promise to counter these headwinds and support 
growth in Asia. The deep integration into global value chains of many Asian economies 
creates scope for AI-enabled gains in logistics, process optimization, and smart manufac 
turing. The technology also offers pathways to accelerate the transition toward higher 
value-added services, potentially enabling countries to leapfrog traditional development 
stages. Most critically, AI is a potential catalyst for augmenting human capabilities and 
reinvigorate productivity growth, especially when demographic trends are constraining 
labor supply growth across much of the region. 
For the purpose of the analysis, we define AI as the engine of modern automation, 
encompassing technologies that perform complex cognitive tasks, either standalone or as 
key components of modern mechanization of both manufacturing and service production. 
This definition includes not only generative AI such as large language models (LLMs), 
but also robotics and more generally physical intelligence. We focus on AI adoption at 
scale—economy-wide deployment of AI that raises the capital share in the aggregate 
production function, as firms and governments invest not only in AI applications but also 
in the enabling physical infrastructure (data centers, specialized chips, cloud platforms) 
needed to deploy the technology broadly. 1 This is distinct from marginal adoption—such 
as firm- or sector-specific subscriptions to language model services—which may boost 
firms’ and sectors’ productivity but does not, by itself, shift factor shares or show up as 
macroeconomic capital deepening. Our modeling of adoption at scale as capital deepening 
with a declining labor share is in the same spirit as Cazzaniga et al. (2024), building on 
Drozd et al. (2022) and Moll et al. (2022). We model AI through this capital-deepening 
channel because it is the channel through which AI bears on the questions we study: 
cross-country divergence, global capital demand, and the distribution of income across 
capital, skills, and generations all operate through forces that shift aggregate factor shares. 

1As AI use scales up, firms and governments may invest in upstream components—such as data centers, specialized chips/accelerators, cloud platforms, and model development/fine-tuning capacity—to secure reliable access to compute, reduce latency and data-governance constraints, and manage cost and supply-chain risks. For example, there are major investments ongoing or planned in Japan and Korea in advanced chip manufacturing, high-bandwidth memory facilities, etc.

AI is a general-purpose technology that is itself embodied in capital—compute, data 
centers, models, and the complementary intangible and organizational capital required to 
make them productive (Brynjolfsson et al., 2021). Deploying AI at scale is therefore an 
act of capital accumulation in the first instance, which raises the capital share directly, 
independent of whether any particular job is displaced. Task automation—AI substituting 
for labor—is one route through which this occurs, but it is not the only one: even 
AI that primarily augments workers is delivered through capital goods and capitalizes 
its productivity gains into higher investment and returns to capital, again manifesting 
as capital deepening. This is precisely why the macroeconomic literature on AI and 
cross-country divergence focuses on channels through factor shares rather than through 
task-level displacement (Alonso et al., 2022; Korinek & Stiglitz, 2019): the capital share 
is the sufficient statistic through which AI’s diverse micro-channels—automation and 
augmentation alike—bear on global capital demand and cross-country income distribution. 
Our capital-deepening representation thus captures AI as a whole, with automation nested 
as a special case, rather than restricting attention to it. 
AI adoption has been uneven so far, raising concerns about potential economic divergence. 
Advanced economies (AEs) appear to move earlier and faster in adopting AI than emerging 
market and developing economies (EMDEs). OECD et al. (2025) documents wide cross 
country gaps in business AI adoption, with AEs generally at the frontier and EMDEs 
lagging behind, and survey-based data also points to strong momentum in enterprise 
uptake of AI with widening cross-country differences. 2 This uneven pace of adoption is 
primarily due to structural differences across AEs and EMDEs, and could cause economic 
divergence (Alonso et al., 2022; Benzell et al., 2021; Cerutti et al., 2025; United Nations 
Development Programme (UNDP), 2025). 
Indeed, Asia exhibits substantial heterogeneity in its preparedness for such adoption 
at scale (Cazzaniga et al., 2024; UNCTAD, 2025; Iida et al., 2026; ). Advanced Asian 
economies (e.g., Singapore and Korea) are near the frontier, and have already begun 
integrating advanced AI systems into production processes, leveraging strong digital 
infrastructure and high human capital. Many EMDEs, by contrast, face structural 
constraints including underdeveloped infrastructure, lower productivity, and a relatively 
low share of skilled workers. For aging economies like Japan and Korea, AI offers crucial 
tools for supporting growth despite shrinking workforces (Asao et al., 2025; Chang et 
al., 2025), while the latter also help mitigate AI-related job displacement. For younger 
economies like India and the Philippines, the challenge lies in ensuring that AI adoption 
creates rather than displaces employment opportunities for growing labor forces. This 
heterogeneity creates a risk of economic divergence across countries: while some countries 

2For example, IBM Global AI Adoption Index in 2023, 2025 Microsoft Work Trend Index and Stanford’s Global AI Index 2025.

are well positioned to harness AI’s benefits, others face the prospect of being left behind. Beyond cross-country divergence, AI adoption at scale could also have distributional consequences within countries. As AI encompasses a broad and evolving set of technologies— from language models to robotics and physical intelligence—the pattern of which tasks are substituted and which are complemented remains highly uncertain and is likely to shift over time. What is clear, however, is that a more capital-intensive production technology will alter the distribution of income between labor and capital, and across worker groups with different degrees of complementarity to the new technology (Cazzaniga et al., 2024). In light of AI’s potential to boost output and productivity and the risk of economic divergence arising from uneven adoption and different exposures, this paper examines the potential impacts of AI adoption across Asian economies. We deploy a small open economy partial equilibrium model with endogenous AI adoption–—adapted from the multi-country framework of Benzell et al. (2021)—–to investigate cross-country AI adoption timing and its macroeconomic, and within-country distributional impacts in the Asia-Pacific region. First, we simulate the cross-country AI adoption paces, and analyze how they are affected by country-specific characteristics.
